sections.html:
Three bodies tax and record a North Huntingdon house on their own schedules, the township, the county and the school district, and the township asks for no resale inspection on an ordinary house sale. North Huntingdon is a first class township in Westmoreland County covering about 27 square miles, governed by a board of commissioners with one commissioner from each of seven wards.

The township had 31,880 residents in 2020 and an estimate of 31,697 for 2025. The Pennsylvania Turnpike (I-76) and the Lincoln Highway (U.S. Route 30) cross it, with the Youghiogheny River touching its southwestern corner.

Owners live in 90.1 percent of the housing units, based on 2020 to 2024 figures, which makes this mostly a township of owned houses. The typical home is worth $232,400. Median household income is $101,200, and 94.4 percent of residents stayed at the same address from the year before, so turnover is low.

Older sections grew around settlements such as Circleville, Cavitt's Mills and Robbin's Station, and the Fullerton Inn and the McFarlane House carry federal historic register listings. Students attend the Norwin School District.

About 21.3 percent of residents are 65 or older, which makes estate sales and downsizing moves a steady source of listings.

The township's permit fee schedule has a residential occupancy permit for new construction only, at $25 and included in the building permit fee. An existing owner-occupied house changing hands doesn't go through an occupancy inspection. Commercial occupancy for a new use or tenant costs $150.

Permits still matter for projects you finish before listing:

  • Residential building permits are charged per square foot plus a state fee and review fee, and the application won't be accepted without a property survey.
  • Accessory buildings under 200 square feet skip the building permit but need a $50 zoning permit.
  • Demolition requires proof of utility shut-offs, and the township inspector checks the sewer cap before backfilling.
  • Inside and outside sanitary sewer inspections on permitted construction are handled by the North Huntingdon Township Municipal Authority.

The Planning and Zoning Department takes questions at 724-863-3806, extension 220, and inspections need 24 hours of notice.

The tax bill multiplies the Westmoreland County assessed value, divided by 1,000, by each millage rate. The levying bodies are the township, the county and the Norwin School District. The township's 2026 budget lists a general real estate rate of 10.73 mills, up from 9.23.

North Huntingdon township levies

General real estate, 20259.23 mills
General real estate, 2026 budget10.73 mills
Fire service fund1.32 mills
Hydrant levy (within 600 feet of a hydrant)0.14 mill
Earned income tax0.50 percent

The same document drops the per capita tax and adds a 2.0 mill increase for the capital reserve fund. Check your own bill for the figures that apply to you.

Since August 1, 2024, Keystone Collections Group has collected the township's occupation tax, local services tax and delinquent real estate tax, and Norwin School District sends its own separate bill. The township tax office on Center Highway handles current township real estate bills.

Each year you may ask the Westmoreland County Board of Assessment Appeals to review your value. Get the filing in by August 1 and any change applies to the next tax year. If a notice of change in assessment arrives, the clock is 40 days from its mailing date.

You can download the form from the county website or pick one up in Greensburg at 40 North Pennsylvania Avenue. Hearings are the second Thursday of each month at 9:00 a.m. in Suite 440.

County values feed the township and school bills alike, so a win lowers all of them at once. Planning to list with an assessment that seems high next to similar nearby houses? File before August 1.

Your deed gets recorded at the Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds, and every document must carry the 10-digit parcel identifier number. Bring original signatures and a certified grantee address, plus the transfer taxes or a finished Statement of Value (REV-183), unless the deed shows a family exemption.

The state's share is 1 percent of the value transferred, and the buyer and seller answer for it jointly. The township's 2026 budget shows real estate transfer tax revenue of $650,000, so a local share applies as well. Ask the Recorder of Deeds for the combined rate on your parcel.

If a deed's transfer tax covers more than one municipality, it must state how the tax is divided.

The fire levy is shared equally among the seven volunteer fire companies inside the township, and a separate hydrant levy applies only within 600 feet of a hydrant. The fire service line appears on every tax bill.

The township maintains about 125 miles of roads, and its 2026 budget stresses roads and stormwater. Sanitary sewer service and inspections run through the North Huntingdon Township Municipal Authority, which you can contact about a lateral line before a buyer's inspector raises it.

With seven wards and three tax bills, paperwork here can scatter. Make a folder for the township bill from the Center Highway tax office, the Norwin School District bill, the county assessment notice and any receipt from Keystone Collections Group. If a delinquent balance went to the collector, call 724-978-0300 for the payoff before a buyer's title search finds it.

Then walk the property with the earlier list in hand. A new deck, a finished basement or a replaced shed may have needed a permit, and a buyer's agent will ask. Tell the Planning and Zoning Department what you did and get the permit closed if it is still open. Having these answers ready keeps a signed contract from stalling.

Owners who value a firm closing date, or who don't want to pay for updates ahead of a buyer's inspection, often choose cash. The buyer takes the house as is, which suits these common cases:

  • A long-held house that needs a new roof, furnace or sewer line.
  • An inherited property that heirs live far from.
  • A home with delinquent township, county or school taxes that moved to a collector.
  • A landlord who wants out of a rental on a short schedule.

The order of work looks much the same on either route. Check with Planning and Zoning on any permit you pulled, collect the current township, county and school bills, and ask your lender for a payoff. The deed then goes to the Recorder of Deeds with the parcel number, original signatures and the transfer tax paid. A cash sale skips the buyer's loan approval and appraisal, so the closing date depends mostly on your title work.

Set any offer next to what a regular listing would net after agent fees, repairs and transfer tax, and read the written purchase terms before you agree.

faqs.q: Does North Huntingdon require a resale occupancy permit?
faqs.a: The residential occupancy permit on the fee schedule is for new construction only, so an ordinary resale of an existing house isn't covered. Call the Planning and Zoning Department at 724-863-3806, extension 220, to confirm for your address.

faqs.q: What is the North Huntingdon real estate tax rate?
faqs.a: The township's general real estate rate is 9.23 mills for 2025 and 10.73 mills in the 2026 budget, plus 1.32 mills for fire service. Westmoreland County and the Norwin School District tax the parcel separately, so check your bill for the full total.

Keystone Collections Group collects the township's occupation, local services and delinquent real estate taxes, and its phone number is 724-978-0300. Norwin School District bills its school taxes separately.

faqs.q: By what date must a Westmoreland County assessment appeal be filed?
faqs.a: Annual appeals are due on or before August 1 and take effect for the next tax year. A notice of change in assessment gives you 40 days from the mailing date to appeal.

faqs.q: How much is transfer tax when selling in North Huntingdon?
faqs.a: Pennsylvania charges 1 percent at the state level, and local shares are added on top. The Westmoreland County Recorder of Deeds can give the combined rate for your parcel before you sign a sales agreement.
